An easy option that many people opt for while they’re on the road is to roam with their home country’s cell phone plan. For some locales, this is a great option. If you’re from a country with more hefty international roaming fees (I believe my Canadian fee is up to $14 CAD/day now), then you’re better off seeking a more reasonably priced phone plan for your travels. [...] 3. Consider how many opportunities there will be for wifi on your trip. If you think you’ll be able to connect to wifi reasonably frequently and have already planned most elements of your trip, I’d recommend purchasing a package with less data (for example, 2GB for a one week trip). Many plans allow you to top up extra GB if you need it. If you think you’ll be coordinating a lot of your trip on-the-go, or could potentially be outside of hotel rooms, cafes, airports, etc. often, then it would be better to start at a 4GB+ plan. If you’ll be somewhere for a while, do know that it becomes more cost effective as you buy bigger plans - so, for example, you could get a 20GB, 180 day global plan for $89 USD (at the time of publication). Nomad's US pricing is in line with other data-only service providers like Airalo and Saily, which charge $4.50 and $4.39, respectively, for 1GB of data over 7 days.

To use Nomad's eSIM service, your device needs to be unlocked and eSIM compatible. Many modern phones, such as the Apple iPhone 16 and the Samsung Galaxy S24, support eSIMs. If you are unsure if your device will work with Nomad, the company lists the phones, tablets, and laptops that are compatible with its service.

Nomad's single-country eSIMs are non-transferable; you will need to install a new eSIM for each country you visit. Thankfully, regional plans provide access to multiple countries with a single eSIM. Meanwhile, Saily allows you to add countries to the same eSIM as needed, simplifying the process. [...] In the US, Nomad offers six regular plans: 1GB for $4.50 (seven days), 1GB for $6 (seven days), 3GB for $11 (30 days), 5GB for $14 (30 days), 10GB for $24 (30 days), and 20GB for $35 (30 days). Though they offer the same 1GB of data, the $4.50 and $6.00 plans are indeed different. The $4.50 plan supports AT&T and T-Mobile and starts automatically when connected to a network or after a 30-day window. The $6.00 plan is limited to just AT&T but provides a more flexible 60-day activation window.

Nomad also offers shorter day plans ranging from 1 to 10 days that come with 1GB of high-speed data per day plus unlimited data throttled to 512Kbps. The website and app clearly outline each plan’s details, and all listed prices include applicable taxes. [...] (Credit: Iyaz Akhtar)

You can view your data usage in the Manage tab of the Nomad app, where you can also see details like when your plan will expire and buy more data. If your data is running low or is set to expire, you will receive a notification. You can purchase additional data at the same price as regular plans. For example, an additional 1GB costs $4.50.

You can choose plans for individual countries, such as China, India, and Japan, or opt for one of the eight regional plans, which include Africa, Asia, and North America. A Global plan covering 105 countries is also available. [...] These prices and policies are competitive with other data-only eSIM providers like Airalo and Nomad. For example, Airalo charges $4.50 for 1GB with seven days of access, and its 30-day plans include 3GB for $11, 5GB for $16, and 20GB for $42. Like Saily, Airalo's data expires at the end of the 7- or 30-day window, and it does not allow you to transfer eSIMs between devices.

Saily relies on roaming partners around the world, which means variable connection quality by region. ## Data plans and pricing

Customers ordering an eSIM have to choose how much data they need and how long they need it for. Saily is flexible on both counts, offering multiple data plans for most destinations.

For example, let's say you are visiting Malaysia. In that case, you can choose one-week or 30-day eSIMs. Data allowances vary from 1 GB for the short plan to 3 GB, 10 GB, or 20 GB for the month-long package. Prices vary depending on your chosen plan, starting at $1.99 per week to $35.99 monthly (with a 20 GB limit) in Czechia, Bulgaria, and Mayotte. [...] Saily also offers regional plans that cross borders. For instance, the European plan covers 36 countries (a much cheaper option than purchasing eSIMs for multiple countries). There are also regional plans for Asia and Oceania (19 countries), Africa (34 countries), Latin America (12 countries), North America (Canada and the USA), and the Middle East and North Africa (19 countries).

The global plan is also worth noting. It's not technically "global" as data plans only cover 113 countries (as of April 2025). Even so, the global plan ranges from Antigua to Iceland. It's a great value option for those with complex travel plans, especially for the year-long plan. [...] Device owners order digital SIMs via the Saily app. Saily then links their device to local network providers wherever they are. Whether you are vacationing in Barbados or traveling in Japan for business, Saily offers immediate internet coverage, often at much lower prices than standard SIMs or eSIM rivals.

Users can also use the Saily ad blocker and web protection, which help limit tracking and reduce the risk of slowdowns or unwanted access. You can also change virtual locations.

## Saily eSIM card: How it works

As you probably know, smartphones and tablets use a physical SIM card to access network coverage. The SIM card (or "Subscriber Identity Module") holds the user's phone number and identification data to make calls or surf the web.

Traveling across Europe has never been easier - but staying connected can still be surprisingly complicated. With dozens of countries, different mobile networks, and wildly inconsistent roaming fees, choosing the right mobile data solution matters more than most travelers expect. This guide compares the most common Europe eSIM providers to help you find the best balance of price, coverage, and reliability.

## What Is an eSIM and How Does It Work in Europe?

An eSIM (embedded SIM) is a digital SIM built directly into your phone. Instead of inserting a plastic card, you install a mobile plan electronically - usually by scanning a QR code or using an app.

  

In Europe, eSIM adoption is particularly strong because:

 Most European carriers support eSIM technology
 Cross-border roaming within Europe is seamless
 Regional data plans can cover dozens of countries

results.title: What's The Best eSIM For Mexico? Here's Our 2025 Ranking
results.content: Once-off prices for eSIMs in Mexico range from $8 to $49 and include between 1 GB and 10 GB of data. Depending on your plan, that's just $4.90 to $8 per gigabyte, which isn't bad for a country like Mexico. Most travellers should be able to get by with these amounts without any problems. Setting up and activating your eSIM happens entirely on your smartphone, and it's very quick. In our test, we just took two minutes (watch our how-to video on YouTube to see how it's done). Moreover, you can easily top this up via the Airalo app if you start running low on data during your trip. This saves you time and hassle compared to buying a physical SIM, where you'd usually need to stand in line at the counter to buy or top up your card or package. [...] Holafly's data packages cost between $19 and $99 once off for trips to Mexico and are valid from five to 90 days. Like Airalo, Holafly's plans in Mexico give you data via local carriers, although this time through Telefónica and Telcel networks. This means you'll get coverage like a local no matter where you travel in the country (however, coverage can still drop in large parts of Mexico like the Andes or Amazon, as we'll see later in this article.) [...] However, one disadvantage is the slightly higher upfront cost than physical SIM cards. That said, eSIMs are still comparatively cheap, especially for use in Mexico from abroad. In our opinion, the significantly higher level of comfort and the possibility of having access to the internet immediately upon arrival are worth the extra pennies. Another disadvantage is related to installation, where the process may be unfamiliar to you if you've never installed an eSIM before. However, if you follow the instructions carefully, you'll be fine.
